en: The Mudgala Upaniṣad: Om! May my speech be established in my mind; may my mind be established in my speech. Be manifest within me.
Be the two nostrils for my Veda; may what I have heard not be lost to me. By this [Veda] which I have studied, I join together days and nights; I shall speak the Ṛta, I shall speak the Truth.
May that protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect the speaker.
First Section.
Oṃ. We shall explain the determination of the meaning of the Puruṣasūkta.
In the Puruṣasaṃhitā, the meaning of the Puruṣasūkta is stated in brief:
in the verse beginning with "sahasraśīrṣā," the word *sa* signifies "infinite."
He spoke of it as being infinite yojanas, and likewise as being ten finger-breadths.
By the first [verse], the pervasion of that Viṣṇu in terms of space is declared;
by the second, the pervasion of this Viṣṇu in terms of time is stated. || 2 ||
Furthermore, Viṣṇu’s role as the bestower of liberation was declared by the third [chapter],
and the majesty of Hari was described by the mantra beginning with "etāvān" (so great).
By this very mantra, the fourfold manifestation is explained;
by the verse beginning with "tripād," the majesty of Aniruddha is proclaimed.
Therefore, by this [verse] beginning with "From Him, Virāṭ," the origin of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa from Hari, who is Pādanārāyaṇa, has been demonstrated. || 5 ||
By this [verse], "yat puruṣeṇa," the sacrifice of creation is proclaimed;
seven are declared to have been its enclosing sticks and its fuel-sticks.
By the mantra "taṃ yajñam," the sacrifice of creation (sṛṣṭiyajña) is proclaimed;
and by this very same mantra, liberation (mokṣa) is also declared. || 7 ||
By the mantra beginning with "tasmāt," the creation of the universe is proclaimed;
by the two mantras beginning with "vedāham," the majesty of Hari is described. (8)
The conclusion with the words "by sacrifice" refers to the creation and the liberation previously described;
for he who understands this thus indeed becomes liberated. || 9 ||
The Second Section.
Now, in the Mudgala Upaniṣad, the majesty of the Puruṣasūkta is expounded in detail.

After Vāsudeva had instructed Indra in the knowledge of the Lord, he further taught Indra—who bowed down again for the sake of subtle hearing—the supreme secret by means of two sections consisting of the Puruṣasūkta. ||1||
Two portions are described.

He who is liberated is the Puruṣa; having abandoned the sphere of name and form—which is beyond the reach of the knowledge of worldly beings and exceedingly difficult for them to comprehend—and desiring to abandon the gods and others afflicted by the *kleśas* and so forth, he assumed an appearance that was auspicious with a thousand parts of a *kalā*, which grants liberation at the mere sight of it.
Having pervaded the worlds beginning with the earth, he stood transcending [them] for infinite *yojanas* in that attire. ||2||
The Person, Nārāyaṇa, was the past, the present, and the future;
he was the bestower of liberation for all,
and he is greater than every greatness.
Therefore, no one is superior. ||3||
The Great Being, having divided himself fourfold, remained with three-quarters in the supreme ether;
with the other, the fourth part, Aniruddha-Nārāyaṇa, all worlds came into being.
And that Pādanārāyaṇa produced Prakṛti in order to create the world.
Being of fully developed body, he did not know how to perform the act of creation.
That Aniruddhanārāyaṇa instructed him in creation.

O Brahman, having meditated upon the senses as the officiating priests, the firm body with its knots as the sacrificial vessel, me as the consumer of the oblation, the spring season as the clarified butter, the summer as the fuel, and the autumn season as the essence—having thus offered [the sacrifice] into the fire, by the touch of the limbs, the body shall be struck down like a thunderbolt. Then, having created all living beings according to their own functions, animals and the like will manifest.
Thereafter, the world consisting of the mobile and the immobile shall come into being. ||5||
By this, it should be understood that the manner of liberation through the union of the individual soul (jīva) and the Self (ātman) has also been explained. ||6||
He who knows this sacrifice of creation and the manner of liberation attains the full span of life. ||7||
The Third Section.
The one God has entered into many forms; though unborn, he is born in many ways. ||1||
The Adhvaryus worship this very [Self] as Agni,
for he joins together all this through the Yajus;
the Chandogas worship it as Sāman.
For in this, all this is established:
"poison" is the serpents;
"serpent" is those who know serpents.
"Ūrj" (vital energy), so say the gods; "rayi" (wealth), so say human beings;
"māyā" (creative power), so say the asuras.
"Self-offering! say the ancestors; "The divine folk! say those who know the divine folk;
"Form! say the Gandharvas.
The Gandharvas are the Apsarases. ||2||
In whatever way one worships it, that is exactly how one becomes.
Therefore, a Brahmin should contemplate: "I am indeed the Supreme Brahman in the form of the Puruṣa.
He becomes of that very nature.
He who knows thus. || 3 ||
The Fourth Section.

That Brahman is beyond the threefold affliction, liberated from the six sheaths, devoid of the six waves, transcending the five sheaths, empty of the six modifications of being; thus it is characterized as being entirely distinct from all such things. ||1||

The threefold suffering, however, consists of the internal (ādhyātmika), the external (ādhibhautika), and the celestial (ādhidaivika); it is of three kinds: namely, the agent, action, and effect; the knower, knowledge, and the object of knowledge; and the enjoyer, enjoyment, and the object of enjoyment. ||2||
Skin, flesh, blood, bone, sinew, and marrow are the six sheaths. ||3||
Lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy constitute the group of six internal enemies. ||4||
The five sheaths are: those consisting of food (annamaya), vital breath (prāṇamaya), mind (manomaya), consciousness (vijñānamaya), and bliss (ānandamaya). ||5||
The six states of being are: birth, growth, transformation, decay, destruction, and [the state of] the beloved. ||6||
Hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death—these are the six waves. ||7||
Family, lineage, birth, caste, stage of life, and form—these are the six delusions. ||8||
Through this yoga, the supreme person becomes the individual soul (jīva), and not otherwise. ||9||
Whoever constantly studies this Upaniṣad becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified by wind;
he becomes purified by the sun.
One becomes free from disease; one becomes prosperous;
and one becomes enriched with sons, grandsons, and so forth.
He becomes wise;
he is purified from the great sins (mahāpātaka);
he is purified from the drinking of liquor (surāpāna).
One becomes purified by approaching those who should not be approached;
one becomes purified by approaching one's mother;
one becomes purified by approaching one's daughter or daughter-in-law.
One becomes purified from the theft of gold; one becomes purified from the failure to honor those born of the Veda;
one becomes purified from failing to serve one's guru.
He becomes purified from officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice; he becomes purified from eating what is unfit to be eaten;
he becomes purified from accepting gifts from the fierce.
One becomes purified from the sin of approaching another's wife;
one becomes unafflicted by desire, anger, greed, delusion, envy, and the like;
and one becomes liberated from all sins.
In this life, one becomes a man. ||10||

Therefore, one should not teach this meaning of the Puruṣasūkta— which is a supreme secret, a royal secret, a divine secret, and more secret than the secret— to one who has not been initiated, nor to one who has not studied the Vedas, nor to one whose nature is not devoted to sacrifice.
Not to one who is not a devotee of Viṣṇu;
not to one who is not a practitioner of yoga;
not to one who speaks excessively.
Not to one who speaks unpleasantly;
not to one who has not studied for a year;
not to one who is dissatisfied.
One should not teach one who has not studied the Vedas. ||11||

The wise teacher, likewise knowing this, having performed breath-control in a pure place under an auspicious constellation and meditating upon the Puruṣa, should instruct the meaning of the Puruṣasūkta into the right ear of the disciple who has approached him;
he should not speak it many times,
for it becomes exhausted by such repetition.
One should instruct [this] repeatedly into the ear.
"The person who, performing this, becomes both a student and a teacher in this very life"—this is the Upaniṣad. 12.
Oṃ! May my speech be established in my mind; may my mind be established in my speech. Be manifest and unconfused within me.
Be the two poles for my Veda; may what I have heard not be lost to me. By means of this study, I join together the days and nights. I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the Truth.
May that protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect the speaker.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Thus ends the Mudgala Upaniṣad.
